title: Israel to deport two Turks arrested in Jerusalem
text: Israel has ordered two of the three Turks who were briefly arrested during Palestinian protests last week to be deported, the Interior Ministry said on Monday. The protests followed U.S. President Donald Trump's recognition of Jerusalem as Israel's capital. The three were detained on Friday on suspicion of assaulting Israeli police near Al-Aqsa mosque in East Jerusalem, which Palestinians regard as the capital of their own future state. An Israeli court released them without charge on Saturday. An Interior Ministry spokeswoman said one of the men was due to be deported later on Monday and the other on Saturday. She said both had entered Israel on Belgian passports. Israeli police had described the three as Turkish tourists. A photograph shared on social media showed them among a group of fez-wearing men and boys outside Al-Aqsa. One of them is seen wearing a Turkish flag T-shirt and waving a Palestinian flag, while two are holding up pictures of Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan. Erdogan has spoken out strongly against Trump's Jerusalem decision, which reversed decades of U.S. policy on the status of a city that is holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims and whose eastern sector Israel captured in the 1967 war. The Interior Ministry spokeswoman said she had no information about the third Turk arrested in the case.

title: Italian police arrest female mafia boss and 24 others in Palermo sweep
text: Police in Palermo, the Sicilian capital, rounded up 25 suspected mobsters on Tuesday on a range of charges, among them a woman accused of standing in as boss for her jailed husband. More than 200 police officers, two helicopters and five canine units took part in the early morning operation. The suspects are accused of extortion, handling stolen goods, vandalism and mafia membership, according to the arrest warrant. Making extensive use of wiretaps and ambient recordings, police pieced together the territorial divisions in the city and the internal power struggle that turned Maria Angela Di Trapani, 49, into a powerful figure in one of the city's historic clans. Her husband is Salvatore "Salvino" Madonia, known as "eyes of ice", who is in jail for murder. Police said she passed messages from her husband to clan members and organized monthly payments to the families of jailed mobsters. She also decided, on behalf of her husband, who should run the mob family's business, or who should be "acting boss". In one wiretap, an accused clan member calls her "the mistress of the house", and the police statement on the arrests said she was the real boss of the Resuttana neighborhood. “For all intents and purposes, she acts like a real man,” a turncoat told investigators, according to the court documents. The Sicilian mafia, or Cosa Nostra, has been weakened by a string of arrests in recent years, particularly compared with the Calabrian Ndrangheta. With many bosses behind bars, their wives have started to take on bigger roles.

title: Inaugural Address Dims Republican Hopes for a More Conservative Trump Agenda
text: Since President Trump's stunning victory, one question has dominated conversations among elected Republicans: Will he really pursue his campaign agenda of nationalism, all but erasing the distinctions that have defined America's political parties for a century? title: Comey lands book deal after abrupt end to FBI career
text: Former FBI Director James Comey, who was fired by U.S. President Donald Trump, has signed a deal for a book about leadership and decision-making that will be published in spring 2018, the publisher said on Wednesday. The deal with Macmillan's Flatiron Books comes three months after Comey's dismissal raised questions about whether Trump tried to interfere with the Federal Bureau of Investigation's probe into Russia's alleged meddling in the U.S. presidential election. Russia denies any interference, and Trump has denied colluding with Russia or interfering with the investigation. The book, which does not yet have a title, will discuss “what good, ethical leadership looks like and how it drives sound decisions,” Bob Miller, president of Macmillan's Flatiron Books, said in a statement on Wednesday. Flatiron won the rights to the book at an auction and did not immediately reply to a request for comment. Along with reflections on Comey's dealings with Trump this year, the book will include anecdotes from his role in leading an investigation into Democrat Hillary Clinton's use of a private email server during her 2016 presidential campaign. Comey's announcement, days before the November election, that the FBI was reopening the Clinton email investigation prompted accusations from some Democrats that he was unfairly influencing the outcome. The FBI eventually closed the probe without taking any action.

title: MARINE VETERAN’S American Flag Burned…Right In His Own Driveway
text: A former Marine and his wife woke up one morning to discover the burned remains of an American flag that used to fly outside their Arizona home. Brian Ellison was backing out of the driveway to head to work on Wednesday morning when he spotted the charred shreds of red, white and blue. “When I looked down, it was the American flag that we fly on the front of our house,” Ellison told KTVK-TV. “It had been burned. It had caught fire. And then I looked at the flagpole and all of the flag had burned off of the pole.” The family has no idea who would do such a thing. “This was not right,” said Ellison's wife, Lisa. “It's personal.” “Somebody may think it's their right to burn the flag, but it doesn't make it right,” said Ellison. Police are investigating the crime. In the meantime, the Ellisons promptly put up their spare flag. “I want everyone in Ahwatukee to get their own flag and all of us stand proud and say this is not going to happen anymore,” said Lisa Ellison.

title: Newest Jobs Report Hides Ongoing Weakness
text: The latest jobs report, released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) on Friday morning, was trumpeted as evidence of an improving economy. The Wall Street Journal said the report “signal[ed] solid momentum in the labor market just days before American voters elect a new president,” while Jeffry Bartash, writing for MarketWatch, said it “shows the seven-year-old economic recovery still has plenty of life despite a slowdown in growth earlier in the year.” A hard look behind the headline numbers, 161,000 new jobs created in October and an unemployment rate of 4.9 percent, reveals a weak economy lagging behind last year's numbers. First, that 161,000 figure was below the 173,000 jobs that Wall Street observers had estimated and predicted. Second, it was far below September's job growth of 191,000. Third, it brought average monthly job growth for the year to just 181,000, compared with 229,000 per month for all of 2015. Additional data points proved the point. So was the labor force participation rate, which remains stuck at 63 percent. In other words, of those available for work, 37 percent aren't working. To put that last number in perspective, at the start of Obama's first term, in January 2009, just over 80 million Americans were not in the labor force. Today that number, as reported by the BLS, is nearly 95 million.

text: A U.S. District Court judge said on Friday she would free former Trump campaign manager Paul Manafort from house arrest once he satisfies certain conditions, saying she was satisfied that the $10 million he agreed to forfeit would be available if he ever failed to show up for court proceedings. The assets cannot be touched without a court order. Once in Florida, Manafort must remain within the area unless he is traveling to Washington for court appearances or meetings with his lawyers, according to the order. title: Cuba has a potential lung cancer vaccine that the US can now test
text: The United States and Cuba have taken big steps toward ending 50 years of hostility, and some researchers believe Americans could gain an unexpected benefit: better access to Cuban medical innovations. “The US may be the world leader in basic cancer research, biotechnology, and treatment,” said Marga Gual Soler, who studies science diplomacy. “But Cuba has built a universal, free, and public health care system, [and] has the highest number of medical doctors per capita in the world, a robust biotechnology industry developed with very low resources, and guaranteed access to drugs and advanced diagnostics for the population.” One of the first diplomatic exchanges involved Cimavax, a lung cancer vaccine first developed in Cuba. But it doesn't work for prevention the way a traditional vaccine does. Instead, it stimulates the immune system in a different way, to stop cancers from growing in people who already have the disease. Researchers there found that the vaccine increased survival rates and caused few side effects in patients with late-stage disease. There is reason for caution: US studies will have to replicate these findings to meet federal regulatory standards, and it is still a long road from clinical trials to wide availability for patients. For now, scientists are excited about the possibility, and the exchange raises questions about how a political shift might spur medical innovation. To find out more, I spoke to Dr. Kelvin Lee of Buffalo's Roswell Park Cancer Institute. Lee helped lead America's collaboration with Havana's Center of Molecular Immunology, which discovered the vaccine. Here, he explains why he thinks Cimavax is especially promising, and why he is so keen on more Cuba-US medical exchanges. Julia Belluz: “How did your exchanges with the Cubans change how you think about medical innovation coming out of there?”

title: Holiday spending hopes lift Amazon, Macy's and other retail shares
text: Shares of Amazon.com Inc, Macy's Inc, Kohl's Corp and other U.S. retailers climbed on Friday on early indications that shoppers are on course to spend more this holiday season than in previous years. Although there were few signs of the frenzy that used to mark the start of the crucial U.S. shopping season, known as Black Friday, industry watchers were optimistic. “The turnout this morning has been relatively slow but it is still the best we have seen in three years,” said Burt Flickinger, managing director of Strategic Resources Group, pointing to improving consumer confidence, a strong job market and healthy housing prices. “We expect it to pick up as the day progresses.” Adobe Analytics forecast online Black Friday sales of $5 billion, which would be a record. Online retailers will take in another $6.6 billion on Cyber Monday, according to Adobe. Amazon, the world's largest online retailer, rose 2.6 percent to a record high, taking its gain in 2017 to nearly 60 percent. It offered its own Black Friday deals and unveiled a preview of its Cyber Monday discounts. Brick-and-mortar stores and their investors are hoping a strong labor market and rising home prices will lift turnout between Thursday's U.S. Thanksgiving holiday and Christmas, a stretch that can account for as much as 40 percent of total annual sales and can make or break a retailer. Wal-Mart Stores Inc, Macy's and others have strengthened their online sales platforms and increased discounts for online orders in an effort to stem market share losses to Amazon.

title: Dem Senator Vows To Filibuster Gorsuch Over Trump’s ‘Looming’ Impeachment
text: Sen. Richard Blumenthal put all his cards on the table when it comes to Donald Trump's Supreme Court nominee, Neil Gorsuch. The Democratic senator from Connecticut argued that, given the looming constitutional crisis facing the country and the growing likelihood that Trump will be impeached, Gorsuch should be filibustered. Speaking from the Senate floor on Monday, Blumenthal said that after careful and deep deliberation, he has decided to vote against Gorsuch. He said that although he still resents the way Republicans treated former President Obama's SCOTUS nominee, Merrick Garland, that is not why he will vote no on Gorsuch. “But my vote is not about Merrick Garland. It is about Neil Gorsuch and it is about the constitutional crisis that may well be looming as a potential threat to our democracy.” Blumenthal pointed to the testimony of FBI Director James Comey, reminding his fellow Senators that Trump is under investigation for possibly colluding with Russia to interfere with the 2016 election. This, he explained, makes the Supreme Court more important than ever. “The independence of our judicial branch has never been more threatened or more important. The possibility of a Supreme Court needing to enforce a subpoena against the president of the United States is far from idle speculation. It has happened before in United States vs. Nixon. President Trump has launched a campaign of vicious and relentless attacks on the credibility of our judiciary. His disparaging comments have attempted to shake the foundations of respect for judicial rulings, the credibility and trust that is so essential to our Supreme Court and all our courts.”

title: Kenyan parliament goes on three-week break at opposition's request
text: A deadlock over how leadership posts should be allocated has forced Kenya's parliament into an unscheduled three-week recess, lawmakers said on Wednesday, a sign that a drawn-out political crisis could reverberate beyond the October election. Kenya, East Africa's most advanced economy and a Western ally against militant Islam, has been gripped by political stalemate since the Supreme Court annulled the results of the Aug. 8 presidential elections on procedural grounds and ordered a re-run. The repeat election took place on Oct. 26, but opposition leader Raila Odinga boycotted the vote, saying it would be unfair. Incumbent President Uhuru Kenyatta won a second, five-year term with 98 percent of the vote. Lawmakers said on Wednesday that Odinga's opposition coalition wanted more time to negotiate how parliamentary leadership posts would be shared among its constituent parties. The National Super Alliance (NASA) coalition has written to the speakers of the national assembly and the senate asking for until the end of November to fill leadership positions in the house, including minority chiefs, whips and committee heads. “The NASA parliamentary group has asked the speaker to give them until end of the month to put their house in order,” Adan Duale, majority leader in the national assembly, said in a text message, adding that parliament would adjourn until Nov. 29. Parliament conducts its business through the Parliamentary Service Commission (PSC) and various committees, which set its calendar and legislative agenda, approve spending and vet key appointments in the executive and the judiciary. Ayub Savula, an opposition legislator, said the delays were caused by disagreements among NASA's four main parties - Odinga's ODM, ANC, Ford Kenya and Wiper - over how to divide the available positions.

title: New Zealand kingmaker party to hold crucial board meeting on Monday
text: The leader of the small New Zealand party that holds the balance of power after last month's inconclusive election said he would hold an important board meeting on Monday as he moves closer to deciding which party he will back in a coalition government. The country has been in political limbo since Sept. 23, when neither the National Party, which has led the government since 2008, nor the Labour Party won enough seats to form a government. New Zealand First has held talks with both over the past week, but has kept the country guessing about which way it is leaning. It convened a caucus on Friday, but the internal meetings were due to continue through Monday. “Members of the board will be ... flying in on Sunday and early Monday morning for a joint caucus and board meeting ... all day Monday,” Winston Peters, leader of the nationalist NZ First Party, told reporters in Wellington. An announcement was expected some time next week. NZ First's policies are closer to those of Labour: both support curbing migration and foreign ownership, renegotiating certain trade deals and changing the central bank's approach to monetary policy. But observers have said a two-way coalition is much easier to put together than one involving three parties. National won 56 seats in the September election, which means it would need only NZ First's nine seats to have a majority in parliament. Labour, with 46 seats, would have to form a coalition with both the Greens and NZ First in order to govern.

While that explains his position, the irony is that Pruitt has no scientific background whatsoever. If he did, he couldn't possibly disagree with this basic scientific fact: regardless of your political position on climate change, carbon dioxide absolutely warms any environment it is found in. Knowing what we now know about the government censoring climate change data in other agencies, it feels like too much to expect this report to come out, or at least to come out unredacted.
